structure.title: The Golden Bird and Hans in Luck · The first two tales play different games with luck
structure.text: In The Golden Bird a king counts his apples and discovers that a thief is taking one each night. Everything depends on catching a loss early. In Hans in Luck a young man makes one trade after another, each of which looks worse to an onlooker and better to Hans. Within a few pages the collection has changed the meaning of good fortune.

structure.title: Jorinda and Jorindel – The Golden Goose · A new tale can usually begin from nothing
structure.text: A hungry household, a locked door or a queen who badly wants a child supplies enough trouble for a new world to start. Characters seldom carry over. An exception is the little sequence about Chanticleer and Partlet, where the same feathered pair take their domestic affairs on the road through three adjacent tales.

structure.title: The Water of Life – Snow-White and Rose-Red · Later tales return to familiar problems with a new rule
structure.text: The Water of Life again gives brothers a quest and a chance to listen to someone unimportant. The Youth Who Went Forth to Learn What Fear Was sends a boy towards precisely the experience most travellers would run away from. Recognising an old pattern is part of the pleasure, especially when this particular hero refuses to do his expected bit.

people.name: The youngest child
people.role: The one who has already seen two attempts fail
people.text: Going last can look like a disadvantage when a father or a king has favourites. It also leaves the youngest a different task from the clever elder brother's. A small act of courtesy to an animal or a stranger may bring information nobody else took the trouble to obtain.

people.name: The animal who knows the road
people.text: The fox in The Golden Bird knows exactly what to choose and what splendid thing to leave untouched. Its advice is hard to follow because the wrong choice looks like the one a reasonable person ought to make. A helper can give a hero excellent information without making the decision for him.

context.title: Repetition gives the listener a head start
context.text: When someone makes three visits to the same place, the listener can begin anticipating the next question or request. A child hearing the story aloud may know exactly what is coming and still be waiting for the one word or gesture that will make this visit turn out differently.

context.title: Familiar tales under unfamiliar English names
context.text: This selection calls Cinderella Ashputtel and uses Snowdrop for the story many readers know as Snow White. A familiar outline can hide a much less familiar scene. Ashputtel's early visits to her mother's grave give the girl's later appeals for help a listener with a history.

notice.text: Inspect the shoes in The Twelve Dancing Princesses.
notice.why: The king has locked the door and believes he knows where his daughters spent the night. Their worn shoes are harder to account for. A whole second life can enter a tale through an ordinary object that ought to have been in better condition in the morning.

passages.quote: their shoes were found to be quite worn through

notice.text: Notice what fits into a kitchen.
notice.why: A mouse, a bird and a sausage can share a household and divide the work. The extraordinary part passes in a sentence. The quarrel about who works hardest receives much more attention, and it is possible to recognise a perfectly ordinary domestic argument before remembering who is conducting it.

notice.text: Listen to the sea when the fisherman goes back with another wish.
notice.why: The fisherman must return to the same water and address the same enchanted fish. The surface and colour of the sea need very few words to register how much has changed since the last request, before the fish gives its answer.

opening: Children are sent into forests, bargains are made with strangers, and a hungry household can become more frightening than the creatures outside it. In the Grimms' tales, danger arrives quickly and survival often depends on noticing a rule, keeping a promise, or accepting help from something easily overlooked. The stories move with a blunt confidence that makes their wonders feel ordinary. A few pages can hold abandonment, terror, ingenuity, and a reversal of fortune extravagant enough to answer a wish everyday life would scarcely permit.
